I.note: A multimeter measures voltage, current and resistance. Before connecting it, set the right function and a range above the expected value, and observe polarity.

q.text: You expect about 12 V DC. What range should you select?
choices: The next range above 12 V, such as 20 V DC
q.why: A range above the expected value, on the right function.

Full.note: An analogue voltmeter is a sensitive meter with a series multiplier resistor; an ammeter has a shunt resistor in parallel. Any meter slightly changes the circuit it measures.

q.text: How is an analogue ammeter's range extended?
choices: With a shunt resistor in parallel
q.why: The shunt carries most of the current.

I.note: A voltmeter has a high resistance and is connected in parallel with what it measures. An ammeter has a low resistance and is connected in series.

q.text: How is an ammeter connected?

I.note: Analogue meters show trends and changes well; digital meters are easier to read precisely. Be able to read both.

q.text: What's an advantage of an analogue meter?
choices: It shows changes and trends easily
q.why: A moving needle shows changes at a glance.

Full.note: Frequency measurements have uncertainties from tolerance, calibration and drift. Allow for these and your signal's bandwidth when operating near a band edge.

q.text: Your counter is accurate to ±1 kHz and your LSB signal is 3 kHz wide. What's the lowest safe dial reading at the bottom of a band starting at 7.000 MHz?
q.why: LSB extends 3 kHz below the dial; add 1 kHz for accuracy.

items.topic: Source and load impedance in test gear

Full.note: A signal generator has a source impedance (usually 50 Ω); its output level depends on the load. Not every instrument has a 50 Ω input: an oscilloscope is usually 1 MΩ. The choice of instrument can affect the measurement.

q.text: A 50 Ω generator is set for 1 V into 50 Ω. What do you see on a 1 MΩ scope input?
q.why: Unloaded, the generator's EMF is twice its matched output.

I.note: DC power in a circuit = voltmeter reading × ammeter reading.

q.text: A transmitter's PA draws 8 A at 13 V. What is the DC input power?

Full.note: Steady RF power can be found from the RF voltage across a dummy load: P = Vrms² ÷ R. AM and SSB power measurements need a steady audio tone. Peak envelope power (PEP) is the average power during the highest peak of the modulation envelope. For a single tone on SSB, PEP equals the average power.

q.text: What's the RF power with 50 V RMS across a 50 Ω dummy load?

Full.note: Crystal calibrators give markers at fixed intervals but need checking against a standard. Digital frequency counters are only as good as their reference. Standard-frequency transmissions (such as MSF at 60 kHz) give a highly accurate reference.

q.text: What limits a frequency counter's accuracy?
choices: The accuracy of its internal reference
q.why: Every reading depends on the timebase.

Full.note: An SWR meter samples the line with either a sense wire alongside the inner conductor or a current transformer and capacitive voltage tap. It separates forward and reflected signals, shown on one switched meter, two meters, or a cross-needle meter that shows both at once.

q.text: What does a cross-needle SWR meter show?
choices: Forward and reflected power at once, with SWR where the needles cross
q.why: Two needles; the crossing point reads SWR.

Full.note: An oscilloscope draws voltage against time. Frequency = 1 ÷ period: count the divisions for one cycle and multiply by the timebase setting. Voltage = divisions × volts per division.

q.text: One cycle spans 4 divisions at 0.5 ms/div. What's the frequency?

Full.note: A spectrum analyser shows amplitude against frequency. The tallest line is the fundamental; harmonics appear at whole multiples of it.

q.text: On a spectrum analyser, a 7 MHz transmitter shows smaller lines at 14 and 21 MHz. What are they?

I.note: Decibels express power ratios: +3 dB doubles the power, +10 dB is ten times; −3 dB halves it. Add decibels to combine gains and losses. dBW is relative to 1 W: 25 W ≈ 14 dBW.

q.text: What power ratio is 13 dB?
A 10 W signal goes through an amplifier with 6 dB gain. What comes out?

Full.note: dB = 10 log(P2 ÷ P1). dBW is relative to 1 W; dBm to 1 mW. For voltages, dB = 20 log(V2 ÷ V1).

q.text: What is 100 W in dBm?
A voltage doubles. How many dB is that?

I.note: Resistor colour code: black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, grey 8, white 9; gold as a multiplier is ×0.1. Tolerance: gold 5%, silver 10%. Four-band: two digits, multiplier, tolerance; five-band: three digits, multiplier, tolerance. Capacitors are often marked with three digits: 103 = 10 × 10³ pF = 10 nF.

q.text: What is a resistor banded yellow, violet, red, gold?
What value is a capacitor marked 104?

Full.note: Temperature changes component values: positive-coefficient parts increase with heat, negative ones decrease. In a tuned circuit this causes drift; cures include using components with opposite coefficients to compensate, or temperature-stable types such as NP0 ceramic capacitors.

q.text: How can temperature drift in a VFO be reduced?
choices: Combine components with opposite temperature coefficients

I.note: Thin metal sheet screening reduces unwanted radiation from equipment and coupling between its stages.

q.text: Why are stages in a transmitter often screened with metal boxes?
choices: To reduce unwanted radiation and coupling

I.note: Soldering joins wires and components using molten solder from a hot iron.

q.text: What is soldering?
q.why: Solder melts at a low temperature and bonds the joint.

I.note: Solder is an alloy with a low melting point. Most contains flux, which helps it flow and prevents oxide forming on the surfaces being joined.

q.text: What does flux do?
choices: Helps solder flow and stops oxide forming

I.note: Some metals solder more easily than others: copper and tinned surfaces are easy; aluminium and stainless steel are difficult.

q.text: Which metal is hardest to solder?

I.note: Clean the iron's tip to remove oxide, then tin it with fresh solder to stop oxide re-forming and to conduct heat well. Tin wires before soldering them for a better joint.

q.text: Why tin the iron's tip?
choices: To prevent oxide and improve heat transfer
q.why: A tinned tip transfers heat efficiently.
